title: Slack apps with Bolt

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, has written a plan for RH-1234 and posted it in the ticket's Slack thread: plan v2, with three buttons under it, Approve, Change and Stop. Somewhere a Temporal run called nova:RH-1234 is waiting for exactly one thing, a decision on that plan. You press Approve.

This morning Temporal is slow, and the button just spins. After a few seconds Slack shows you a small error, so you do what everyone does and press Approve again. Did Nova get your approval once, twice, or not at all? And while you were waiting, could your teammate Dana have pressed Approve on a plan she never asked for?
hook.question: How does a click in Slack reach the waiting run quickly, exactly once, and with the right person's name on it?

p: Three things take part in every click. Slack is where people talk and press buttons. Temporal holds the run nova:RH-1234, which is waiting for a signal (a message to a running workflow, from the lessons on Temporal). Between them sits our Slack app, a small Node program built with Bolt, Slack's official framework for apps. The app is a translator: everything that comes from Slack, whether a slash command, a button click or a reply in a thread, becomes one Temporal call, and the call always says who did it.

Most Slack apps give Slack a public URL, and Slack sends every click there. Ours runs in Socket Mode instead, which turns the direction around: the app opens a WebSocket (a connection that stays open in both directions) to Slack, and Slack sends the clicks down that connection. We publish no URL at all, so there is nothing on the internet for an attacker to call, which is the same reason the Jira poll asks Jira instead of waiting for Jira to call us.

Socket Mode needs two tokens. The app-level token starts with xapp- and has one scope, connections:write, which allows it to open the socket. The bot token starts with xoxb- and calls Slack's Web API, for example chat.postMessage to post a message.

notes.text: The bot token (xoxb-): used for every Web API call the app makes.
The app-level token (xapp-): used only to open the socket.
ack() tells Slack the command arrived. The next section is about why it comes first.
Slack knows a person by a member ID like U0123ABCD. A small file maps it to the same person's Jira and GitHub names.
The same startRun as the Jira poll, so /nova RH-1234 joins the run that is already open.
respond() answers only the person who typed the command; nobody else in the channel sees it.

p: When Slack sends your app a command or a click, it waits at most three seconds for an acknowledgement. In Bolt you send it by calling ack(). If ack() does not arrive in time, Slack stops waiting and shows the person an error, even if your code finishes the work a moment later. That is the scene from the story: the approval did reach the run, but Slack had already told you it failed, so you pressed again.

So every handler starts with await ack(), and only then talks to Temporal, Jira or Slack's API, which can take as long as they need. Bolt also notices a late ack and writes an error to the app's log, which you will see in the lab: An incoming event was not acknowledged within 3 seconds. A second time limit hides in the same place. A click carries a trigger_id, which the app needs to open a modal (a pop-up form inside Slack, used by the Change button), and a trigger_id also expires after three seconds.
read.see: [ERROR]  bolt-app An incoming event was not acknowledged within 3 seconds. Ensure that the ack() argument is called in a listener.

read.h: A button that knows its run
p: Slack messages with buttons are written in Block Kit, Slack's JSON format for message layout: a list of blocks such as a section of text or a row of buttons. Each button has two fields that matter to us. The action_id says what the button does, and the app listens for it. The value is free text for our own use, and we put the run's address in it: nova:RH-1234|v2, the workflow ID and the plan version.

The version is there because plans change. If you press Change, Nova writes plan v3 and posts it with new buttons, but the old v2 message is still in the thread. An old button carries v2 in its value, so the run can see that the approval is for a plan it no longer has and ignore it.

code.file: the actions block of the plan message

notes.text: action_id: the name the app's handler matches.
value: which run and which plan version this button decides.

read.h: One click, one signal, one name
p: Now the handler for the Approve button. It answers Slack first. Then it reads the value to find the run, and looks up who clicked. Slack tells us the clicker's member ID, which we map to a person, and only the requester, the person who handed the ticket to Nova, may decide a plan; anyone else gets an ephemeral message, a message that only they can see. Then the handler sends the decidePlan signal with the person's name and the plan version, and finally edits the message with chat.update so it says who approved and has no buttons left.

That last step is what makes a second click harmless. A message without buttons cannot be clicked again, and the run also ignores a decision that arrives after it has one. If Temporal cannot be reached at all, the handler tells the person to try again in a minute, because a decision must never disappear without anyone knowing.

notes.text: The same handler type serves many kinds of actions; this narrows it to a button click in a message.
The value from the Block Kit JSON: "nova:RH-1234|v2" becomes the run and the version.
Who may decide is checked here, before anything reaches the run.
The signal carries the person and the version, so Jira and the PR can say who approved which plan.
ts is the message's ID in Slack, a timestamp string like 1760364000.123456. With the channel, it names the exact message to edit.
blocks: [] removes the buttons, so the same decision cannot be sent twice.

deeper.h: Go deeper: one status message, and replies as answers
p: Each ticket gets one thread in the Nova channel. Its first message is the status line (Checking, Planning, Awaiting approval, Working, PR open), and the app keeps it current with chat.update on the same channel and ts, instead of posting a new message at every step. A reply inside the thread is chat.postMessage with thread_ts set to that first message's ts.

When Nova asks a question, the answer is a person's reply in that thread. The app listens to message events with app.event("message") and keeps only real replies: no subtype (which would mean an edit or a join), no bot_id (which would be a bot, Nova included), and a thread_ts that belongs to a run. Each reply becomes the answerQuestion signal with the text and who wrote it. Without the bot_id filter, Nova's own questions would count as answers to themselves.

lab.title: A button that reaches the run once
lab.goal: Run a real Bolt app on your laptop, play Slack yourself, and see an Approve click become one signal, then break and repair the three-second rule.

guess.q: A teammate moves await ack() to the end of the Approve handler, "so Slack only says OK once Nova really has the approval". Temporal takes four seconds today. What does the person see?

options.text: A short wait, then the message changes to "approved".
options.why: Slack stops waiting after three seconds. By the time ack() runs, Slack has already given up, and in the lab the message is never edited at all.

options.text: An error in Slack, even though the run did get the approval, and the button is still there to click again.
options.why: The signal went out, but ack() was too late. The person sees a failure, the buttons stay, and a second click is the natural reaction.

options.text: Nothing, because Bolt calls ack() for you after three seconds.
options.why: Bolt never acknowledges for you. It only writes an error to the log that the event was not acknowledged in time.

follow.say: Socket Mode needs a real Slack workspace, so in this lab your laptop plays Slack instead. The app uses Bolt's HTTP mode, where the handlers are exactly the same lines; only the constructor changes. Start with a folder and Bolt itself.

Create the app: the /nova command posts plan v2 with an Approve button, and the button handler sends one signal and edits the message. Temporal is replaced by a stand-in that only prints, so you can focus on Slack.
Start the pretend Slack in the first terminal and the app in the second, and leave both open.

lab.build: Right now anyone can approve Sean's plan: try node slack.mjs click U_DANA and watch a click by Dana, a teammate who did not ask for the ticket, become a signal. Change app.mjs so only the requester decides. When /nova starts a run, remember who typed it (command.user_id) for that workflow ID. In the button handler, if body.user.id is not that person, send client.chat.postEphemeral({ channel, user, text }) saying who can decide, and return without a signal. Restart the app, run the command again, then click as U_DANA and as U_SEAN.
checks: node slack.mjs click U_DANA prints chat.postEphemeral in terminal 1 and no signal in terminal 2.
node slack.mjs click U_SEAN prints one decidePlan signal with version 'v2' and a chat.update with an empty set of buttons.
Every "app answered" line says fine, well under 3000 ms.
With ack() moved below the signal and TEMPORAL_MS=4000, the app log shows "not acknowledged within 3 seconds"; with ack() first again, it does not.
lab.fix: A teammate moved await ack() below the signal "so Slack only says OK when Nova really has it". Make that change in app.mjs, restart the app with TEMPORAL_MS=4000 node app.mjs to make Temporal slow, and click as U_SEAN. The script says the app took over 3000 ms, the app log shows Bolt's not-acknowledged error, and terminal 1 shows no chat.update, so the button is still there to click again. Put ack() back on the first line and click again.
explain: Why must ack() come before the Temporal call, even though the Temporal call is the important part?
What two things stop a second click on Approve from approving twice?
Why does the button's value carry the plan version, and not only the workflow ID?
lab.done: Dana's click gets a private refusal, Sean's click gives one signal and removes the button, and you stopped both servers with Ctrl+C.

check.q: Your /nova handler starts the run first and calls ack() after. Starting the run takes four seconds. What happens?

options.text: The run starts, but the person sees an error, because Slack stopped waiting after three seconds
options.why: Slack needs the acknowledgement within three seconds. The work finished, but the person was already told it failed, and will probably try again.

options.text: Slack waits for the run to start, then shows the reply
options.why: Slack does not wait for your work. It waits only for ack(), and only for three seconds.

options.text: Bolt acknowledges for you, so nothing goes wrong
options.why: Bolt never acknowledges for you. It only logs that the event was not acknowledged in time.

check.q: Why does the app edit the plan message with chat.update after a decision?

options.text: Because Slack deletes a message with buttons after one click
options.why: Slack keeps the message and its buttons forever unless the app changes them.
It costs one extra call. The reason is safety, not cost.

options.text: So the message shows who decided and has no buttons left to send the decision a second time
options.why: A message without buttons cannot be clicked again. The run also ignores a late decision, so a second click does nothing either way.

check.q: Your teammate Dana presses Approve on Sean's plan for RH-1234. What should the app do?

options.text: Send the signal, because any teammate may approve a plan
options.why: Only the requester decides a plan, because the plan says what "done" means for the person who asked.

options.text: Show Dana a message only she can see, saying who can decide, and send nothing to the run
options.why: The check happens in the app, before the run hears anything. The run stays waiting for Sean.

options.text: Remove the buttons so nobody can approve
options.why: Then Sean could not approve either. Only a real decision removes the buttons.

p: Our Slack app lives in slack-app/ in the ai-agents repo and runs on inf-rhinohealth in Socket Mode, with both tokens from Vault at infrastructure/ai-agents/slack-app. It offers /nova RH-1234, /nova status and /nova stop, and keeps one status message per ticket in the Nova channel, edited in place. Its channel and ts become the run's Slack scope in the broker, so a run may post only in its own thread.

/nova RH-1234 does not start the run directly in the end: it maps the Slack user to a Jira accountId through config/people.yaml, records them as the requester on the ticket, and assigns the ticket to Nova, so the Jira poll starts the run the same way for both paths. Plan buttons carry the workflow ID and plan version, and only the requester's decision counts.

tickets.why: The Bolt app in Socket Mode, the /nova verbs, ack first, and one status message edited with chat.update.
Every button and thread reply becomes a signal that records who did it; buttons disappear after a decision.
The plan message's Block Kit buttons carry nova:RH-1234|v2, and only the requester's click counts.
/nova maps the Slack user through config/people.yaml and hands the ticket over in Jira.

words.plain: The app opens a WebSocket to Slack, so Slack never needs a public URL of ours.
Tells Slack the request arrived. It must happen within three seconds, before the slow work.
Slack's JSON format for message layout: sections of text, rows of buttons, and more.
The name of a button's action; the app's handler listens for it.
A Slack message's ID, a timestamp string. With the channel it lets you edit the message or reply in its thread.
A message only one person in the channel can see.

review.q: Write the first three lines of any Bolt button handler from memory, in the right order.
review.a: await ack(); narrow the types (block_actions and button); read action.value to find the run. ack() always comes first.

review.q: A teammate asks why we don't just give Slack a public URL like most apps. What do you answer?
review.a: Socket Mode lets the app dial out over a WebSocket, so we publish nothing on the internet that anyone could call. The same reason we poll Jira instead of receiving webhooks.

review.q: Sean pressed Approve twice because Slack showed an error. Name the three things that keep that from becoming two approvals.
review.a: ack() first so the error does not happen; chat.update removes the buttons after the decision; and the run ignores a decision once it has one (and an old version).

remember: Answer Slack within three seconds, then turn each click into one Temporal call that names the person, and remove the buttons once it is decided.
